title: Guppy Breathing Fast? Test Ammonia and Oxygen First
description: A guppy breathing fast is usually reacting to ammonia, nitrite, low oxygen or heat. What to test first, when it is gill flukes, and how to fix it today.
h1: Guppy Breathing Fast or Gasping: Water, Oxygen or Gill Parasites?
howto_name: How to find out why a guppy is breathing fast and fix it
short_answer: Fast breathing in a guppy almost always means its gills are struggling, and the usual reasons are ammonia or nitrite in the water, too little oxygen, or water that is too warm. Test ammonia and nitrite and add aeration today. If the water is clean and well aerated and the guppy keeps breathing hard, flashing or clamping its fins, gill parasites such as flukes are next on the list.
intro: Guppies breathe by pumping water over their gills, and when those gills are damaged or the water carries too little oxygen, the fish pumps faster. That is why rapid breathing is one of the earliest and most reliable warning signs in a guppy tank. Ammonia burns the gill tissue, nitrite stops the blood carrying oxygen, and warm or stagnant water simply holds less oxygen to begin with.[1][2] In most cases the problem is the water, not a disease, and it can be fixed the same day.

Guppies also have a built-in emergency behaviour that owners often misread. When oxygen runs low they hang just under the surface with their mouths at the water line, skimming the thin, oxygen-rich top layer — a behaviour called aquatic surface respiration.[4] If your guppies are breathing fast and crowding at the surface, the tank is short of oxygen or something is stopping their gills from using it. If one guppy is breathing fast while the rest look fine, the cause is more likely to be in that fish: parasites, infection, or stress.
causes_h2: Why Is My Guppy Breathing Fast? The Common Causes

causes.title: Ammonia or Nitrite in the Water
paragraphs: This is the most common cause, particularly in a tank that is less than two months old, overstocked, overfed, or has recently had its filter cleaned too hard. Ammonia damages the gills even at levels that seem tiny: tissue damage has been seen when the toxic un-ionized form exceeds 0.05 mg/L.[1] A veterinary review of water-quality problems in ornamental fish lists the signs of ammonia poisoning as extra mucus, red or bleeding gills, darker body colour, gasping at the surface and an increased breathing rate.[2] Guppies are usually kept in hard, alkaline water, and the toxic fraction of ammonia rises as pH and temperature rise,[3] so a reading that would be mild in soft, acidic water can be significant in a guppy tank.

Nitrite works differently. It is absorbed through the gills and converts haemoglobin into methaemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen — the condition is called brown blood disease because the blood and gills turn brown.[1][2] A fish with nitrite poisoning can be surrounded by oxygen and still suffocate, which is why it breathes fast even in a well-aerated tank. Nitrite spikes are typical of the second half of a new tank's cycle.

causes.title: Low Oxygen or Water That Is Too Warm
paragraphs: Warm water holds much less dissolved oxygen than cool water,[5] while at the same time warmer water speeds up a guppy's metabolism so it needs more. A tank that creeps above about 28 °C in a heatwave, or one with a stuck heater, can run short of oxygen quickly, especially if it is crowded or has little surface movement. Oxygen is also lowest at night and first thing in the morning, when plants stop producing it but everything in the tank keeps using it,[5] so fish that are gasping at dawn and seem better by afternoon are a classic sign of marginal oxygen.

Guppies are well adapted to cope for a while. In laboratory studies they started skimming the surface once oxygen fell to roughly a third of normal, and spent more and more of their time there as oxygen dropped further; guppies prevented from reaching the surface died within minutes to hours at levels they could survive for much longer when allowed to skim.[4] The same research found that females spent more time at the surface than males, and that larger females did so more — so a big, heavily pregnant female is often the first fish you see breathing hard at the top.[4] Hypoxic fish gather near the surface and gulp, a behaviour called piping.[1]

causes.title: Gill Parasites (Flukes, Trichodina, Ich, Velvet)
paragraphs: If the water tests clean and the tank is well aerated, parasites on the gills are the next suspect. Monogenean flukes are the classic example: infected fish flash and rub against objects, breathe rapidly, and hold their gill covers flared, showing swollen, pale gills.[6] Guppies are well-known hosts of Gyrodactylus flukes, and a national survey of ornamental fish in India still found Gyrodactylus on guppies sold in aquarium markets despite the country's quarantine requirements.[7] Flukes are too small to see with the naked eye, so the clue is fast breathing combined with flashing, clamped fins and a fish that looks slightly ragged.

Other gill parasites cause the same picture. Trichodina causes a high breathing rate, gasping at the surface, excess mucus and flashing.[6] Ich (white spot) can infect the gills before any white spots appear on the body, leaving the gills pale and swollen and the fish breathing hard.[8] Velvet gives the skin a fine gold or brownish dusting and can kill quickly.[6] Parasites usually arrive with new fish, so suspect them most if you have added fish or plants in the last few weeks.

causes.title: Chlorine, Chemicals or Medication
paragraphs: Chlorine and chloramine from tap water are highly toxic to fish: harm starts at concentrations as low as 0.02 mg/L.[1] Rapid breathing that starts within minutes to hours of a water change points straight at a missed dose of dechlorinator, or at a water supply that has switched to chloramine. Sudden temperature differences between old and new water add to the stress.[1]

Other culprits are household sprays and cleaning products near the tank, new ornaments or rocks that leach chemicals, and medications — some treatments lower oxygen or irritate the gills, and some antibiotics damage the filter bacteria, which then lets ammonia rise.[3] If all the fish started breathing hard after something was added, remove it and change water.

causes.title: Short-Term Stress, Late Pregnancy or a Fish That Is Dying
paragraphs: Some fast breathing is normal. A guppy that has just been chased by a male, netted, moved to a new tank or has been giving birth will breathe hard for a while and settle within an hour or so. Late-pregnant females are large and carrying a heavy load, and as the research above shows, big females are the ones most likely to use the surface when oxygen is marginal.[4]

At the other end of the scale, rapid, laboured breathing is a common final sign of many serious illnesses. A guppy that is breathing fast while lying on the bottom, not eating and losing colour is often in the last stage of a bacterial or other systemic disease. That fish still deserves a water test, because the same conditions may be harming the rest of the tank.

diagnose_h2: How to Find Out Why Your Guppy Is Breathing Fast
diagnose_intro: Do these checks in order. The first three find the cause in most tanks and take less than half an hour.

diagnose.detail: Watch the gill covers of the affected guppy and several others for a minute. If every fish is breathing fast or hanging at the surface, the problem is the water or oxygen. If only one fish is affected, it is more likely to be something in that fish — parasites, infection or pregnancy — though you should still test the water.

Both should read zero in an established tank. Any ammonia or nitrite is a problem when fish are breathing fast.[3] Check pH too: the same ammonia reading is more dangerous at higher pH and temperature.[3] If you have a dip-strip kit, confirm a positive result with a liquid test if you can.

Guppies do best at about 22–28 °C. Read the thermometer, check the heater is not stuck on, and look at the surface: it should be rippling, not still. Fish that are worst early in the morning and better later in the day point to low oxygen overnight.[5]

Water change (was dechlorinator added?), new fish or plants, new decorations, cleaning products or sprays nearby, a medication added, or a filter cleaned or switched off. Sudden breathing problems after any of these point to that change.[1]

Watch for flashing (fish rubbing or darting against objects), clamped fins, excess mucus making the skin look cloudy, white spots, or a fine gold dust on the body.[6][8] Fast breathing with flashing in clean water strongly suggests gill parasites. A vet can confirm flukes or Trichodina by looking at a gill or skin sample under a microscope.

diagnose.action: Check the fish for other signs of illness
diagnose.detail: Note whether the guppy is eating, whether its colour has faded or darkened, and whether there are red streaks, ulcers or raised scales. Darkened colour and gasping together fit ammonia exposure.[2] A fish that is thin, pale and lying on the bottom is likely to have a serious systemic illness.

fix_h2: What to Do for a Guppy That Is Breathing Fast

fix.detail: Add an air stone, turn up the filter or point its outflow at the surface so the water ripples. This helps whatever the cause and is safe to do before you know it. If the tank is too warm, lower the temperature gradually rather than with a sudden cold water change, because abrupt temperature swings are themselves a stress.[1][5]

fix.action: If ammonia or nitrite is present: change water and cut feeding
fix.detail: Change 25–50% of the water with dechlorinated water at the same temperature, and stop feeding or feed very lightly for a day or two so less waste is produced.[3] Repeat daily until readings are zero. Do not clean the filter media hard; rinse it gently in removed tank water if it is clogged. Chloride competes with nitrite at the gills,[1] which is why some keepers use a small amount of aquarium salt during a nitrite spike — follow the product label and remember that salt treats the fish, not the cause.

fix.action: If a water change was the trigger: dechlorinate and match temperature
fix.detail: Check that your water conditioner removes chloramine as well as chlorine, dose it for the full tank volume, and match the temperature of new water to the tank. Chlorine is toxic at very low concentrations,[1] so a second, correctly treated water change is often the quickest fix.

fix.action: If the water is clean: treat for gill parasites
fix.detail: For confirmed or strongly suspected flukes, praziquantel in a prolonged bath is the treatment of choice in freshwater ornamental fish — use a commercial product and follow its label.[6] For ich, treatments must be repeated because only the free-swimming stage is vulnerable, and at typical guppy temperatures the parasite's life cycle takes only a few days.[8] Treat the whole tank, not just one fish, and keep aeration high during treatment.

Many gill parasites arrive on new fish. Keep new guppies in a separate tank for at least 30 days before adding them, watching for flashing, fast breathing and white spots.[9] Surveys show that parasites still turn up on ornamental fish that have passed through official quarantine,[7] so your own quarantine is worth the effort.

prevention: Cycle a new tank fully before adding guppies, add fish gradually, and do regular partial water changes so ammonia and nitrite stay at zero.[3] Feed only what the fish eat in a minute or two. Keep the surface moving with the filter outflow or an air stone, especially in warm weather and in crowded tanks, and keep the temperature within the guppy range of about 22–28 °C.[5] Always dechlorinate new water,[1] rinse filter media gently in tank water rather than tap water, and quarantine new fish and plants for at least 30 days.[9]
seek_help_h2: When Fast Breathing Needs Expert Help
seek_help: This is an emergency if: several guppies are gasping at the surface, lying on the bottom, or have died in the last day — add aeration and change water immediately, then test.[1] Get help from an aquatic vet or experienced fish shop if: the water tests clean and fish keep breathing fast with flashing or clamped fins; a microscope examination of the gills can identify flukes or other parasites so that you treat the right thing.[6] A single guppy that breathes hard for a few minutes after being chased and then settles does not need treatment.

faq.q: Why is my guppy breathing fast at the top of the tank?
faq.a: Hanging at the surface with rapid gill movements usually means the guppy is short of oxygen. Guppies skim the oxygen-rich top layer of water when oxygen is low,[4] and they do the same when ammonia or nitrite stops their gills working properly.[2] Add aeration straight away and test the water.

faq.q: Why is my guppy breathing fast at the bottom of the tank?
faq.a: A guppy that lies on the bottom breathing hard is usually more seriously unwell than one at the surface. It can still be water quality — ammonia poisoning causes lethargy as well as fast breathing[1] — but it also fits advanced parasitic or bacterial disease. Test the water, change some of it, and look closely for other signs.

faq.q: Is it normal for a pregnant guppy to breathe fast?
faq.a: A female close to giving birth, or in the middle of it, may breathe harder for a while. Large females are also the first to show surface breathing when oxygen is marginal,[4] so a pregnant female gasping at the top can be an early warning about the tank rather than about her. If she keeps breathing fast for more than a few hours, test the water.

faq.q: Why are my guppies breathing fast after a water change?
faq.a: The usual reasons are chlorine or chloramine that was not neutralised, a large difference in temperature, or a change in pH. Chlorine harms fish at very low concentrations.[1] Add aeration, check that you used a conditioner that handles chloramine at the right dose, and match the temperature next time.

faq.q: Can I tell if my guppy has gill flukes without a microscope?
faq.a: Not for certain. Flukes are too small to see, but they cause a recognisable pattern: rapid breathing, flared gill covers, flashing against objects and clamped fins, in water that tests clean.[6] A vet can confirm them from a gill or skin sample.

faq.q: Will aquarium salt help a guppy breathing fast?
faq.a: Only in specific cases. Chloride reduces how much nitrite the gills absorb,[1] so salt can help during a nitrite spike, and salt baths are one option for ich.[8] Salt does not fix ammonia, low oxygen or heat, and the underlying water problem still has to be solved. Follow the product label for any dose.
